query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a trace amount (~0.1 at.%) of carbon to a refractory high‐entropy alloy will enable in situ precipitation of fine carbides at high operating temperatures, thereby reinforcing the matrix and enhancing high-temperature yield strength without altering the room-temperature microstructure and ductility or significantly increasing density.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase refractory HEA (e.g., Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20) with a disordered solid solution state that shows good room-temperature ductility but limited high-temperature strength.
generation.intervention: Introduce a low carbon addition (approximately 0.1 at.%) during alloy synthesis.
generation.conditions: Under service conditions typical of jet turbine applications, i.e., high temperatures (above ~800 °C) during operation and ambient conditions during handling; the intervention should not affect room-temperature properties.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ formation of nano-scale carbides (e.g., Ta3C and Nb3C) upon exposure to high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, a controlled diffusion of carbon promotes carbide precipitation which impedes dislocation motion (precipitation strengthening) and thereby increases the yield strength, while at room temperature the low carbon level does not trigger phase changes, preserving the baseline ductile microstructure and keeping density virtually unchanged.
generation.predicted_outcome: A measurable improvement in high-temperature yield strength relative to the undoped alloy (with the baseline performance of, for example, NbMoTaW-type RHEAs), while room-temperature mechanical properties (ductility and strength) remain essentially unaltered and the alloy density does not increase significantly.
generation.baseline: The refractory HEA without carbon addition that exhibits high-temperature performance limitations and acceptable room-temperature properties.
generation.boundary: The positive effects are expected only within a narrow carbon concentration window; excessive carbon could lead to excessive carbide formation, embrittlement at room temperature, or density increases, and the strengthening mechanism may be less effective at temperatures that are too low to trigger carbide precipitation.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence indicates that trace carbon can induce carbide formation under high-pressure and high-temperature conditions, the exact kinetics of carbide precipitation under typical jet turbine operating pressures and temperature gradients and the quantitative improvement in yield strength remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two batches of the targeted refractory HEA (e.g., Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20): one undoped and one doped with 0.1 at.% carbon. Process both batches identically. Conduct standardized tensile tests at room temperature and in the high-temperature range (e.g., 800 °C to 1000 °C) to assess yield strength, ductility, and any phase changes. Microstructural analyses (XRD and TEM) before and after high-temperature exposure will verify carbide precipitation in the doped alloy.
measurements: Room-temperature yield strength and ductility (% elongation)
Phase composition and identification of nano-precipitates via XRD/TEM
Density measurements to confirm negligible increase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the carbon-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature yield strength (with no significant detrimental effects on room-temperature ductility and density) compared to the undoped baseline, or if unexpected phases form at room temperature, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In this work, the formation of carbide with the concertation of carbon at 0.1 at.% in refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20 was studied under both ambient and high-pressure high-temperature conditions. The x-ray diffraction of dilute carbon (C)-doped RHEA under ambient pressure showed that the phases and lattice constant of RHEA were not influenced by the addition of 0.1 at.% C. In contrast, C-doped RHEA showed unexpected phase formation and transformation under combined high-pressure and high-temperature conditions by resistively employing the heated diamond anvil cell (DAC) technique. The new FCC_L12 phase appeared at 6 GPa and 809 °C and preserved the ambient temperature and pressure. High-pressure and high-temperature promoted the formation of carbides Ta3C and Nb3C, which are stable and may further improve the mechanical performance of the dilute C-doped alloy Mo15Nb20Re15Ta30W20.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), which are considered as a new class of advanced metallic materials, are drawing increasing attention because of their promising properties [,,], such as high strength at both room temperature and elevated temperatures [,], exceptional ductility [], and toughness []. HEAs were initially defined as alloys containing five or more elements with equal or near-equal concentrations [], while the later studies expended HEAs to include minor elements []. Many studies on HEAs were motivated by the possibility that properties may be tunable based on the elements contained in the HEAs. For example, Al-based HEAs [,,,] were studied for application on aircraft engines and nuclear reactors because of their low densities. On the other hand, because of the high melting temperature and high hardness of W and Re, HEAs that contained W or Re were expected to maintain advanced mechanical properties for high-temperature applications [,].
